description: Looking for passionate members skilled in programming, AI, engineering, research, and design. Creativity and teamwork are welcome!
summary:
Sky Hunters is a browser game and explorer that lets anyone search real NASA SPHEREx images for things that change in the sky. Guided by two characters, Nova the astronomer and Sphe the telescope, players learn the “blink” method that helped find Pluto: flip between two pictures of the same patch of sky and spot what moved.

We built it from real SPHEREx DR1 spectral images retrieved from NASA/IPAC IRSA. It covers three fields (WISE 0855, Barnard’s Star and Epsilon Indi), six detectors (0.75–5.0 µm) and two epoch pairs per detector, about six months and about one year apart. Players can blink, view differences, zoom and click a star to see its real spectrum. In two rounds, players find where a star has moved since its year‑2000 catalog position. In two other rounds, we add a simulated variable star to a real image, and the game labels it as simulated.

It matters because it turns a complex survey archive into an approachable activity, building curiosity about time-domain astronomy and the infrared sky.
details:
Sky Hunters turns real NASA SPHEREx infrared images into a game and a small data tool that teaches how astronomers spot things that move or change in the sky.

What it does. For three fields (WISE 0855, Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi), the game shows two real SPHEREx observations of the same patch of sky about six months apart (177 to 201 days, depending on the detector), with the real dates under each image. Players “blink” between the two images, as astronomers did with photographic plates. In two rounds they find where a star really is today compared with its catalogue position in the year 2000 (proper motion). In two rounds they find a simulated variable star hidden in real images, clearly labelled as simulated. Explore mode lets users enter RA/Dec, pick one of the six SPHEREx detectors (0.75 to 5.0 µm), compare epochs or a difference image, zoom, read observation metadata, and click a star to plot its spectrum at the real wavelengths of the frames. A short illustrated story with two characters and spoken narration explains the idea first, in simple English for children.

Impact. It makes a real survey dataset easy to understand and fun, with no installation, and invites people to explore the SPHEREx archive themselves.

Tools. SPHEREx spectral images from NASA/IPAC IRSA; Python (astropy, numpy, scipy, Pillow) in a local viewer that downloads, resamples and stacks frames; target coordinates from SIMBAD; one HTML/CSS/JavaScript file using Canvas, inline SVG and browser speech synthesis, hosted on GitHub Pages. [AI assistance: Claude helped write and debug code and text. Edit to match your rules.]

Creativity. A research technique becomes a story, a hunt and a data tool in one page, and every simulated element is labelled honestly.

What we considered. Accuracy (instrument numbers and proper motions checked against published sources), the fact that SPHEREx’s revisit timing makes gaps near, but not exactly, six months, a design that needs no server so it works offline from the archive, and clear language for young players.

Limitations. The web version holds three prepared fields, not a live search for any coordinates. Spectrum values are background-subtracted image units, not calibrated flux. Live search and Gaia/WISE overlays need a small server, which is our next step.
